chunks.text: The rubber fig, also called the Indian rubber tree, is a large banyan-type fig native to a band of eastern South and Southeast Asia running from Nepal and northeast India through Myanmar, Thailand and Yunnan into Malaysia and Indonesia, where mature wild trees typically grow 30 to 40 metres tall, occasionally more, supported by thick buttressing and aerial roots and bearing broad, glossy oval leaves that can reach 45 centimetres on young plants though mature trees usually show smaller, roughly 10-centimetre leaves. Every part of the plant exudes a milky latex, and before the Brazilian Pará rubber tree, Hevea brasiliensis, was introduced to Asian plantations in the late nineteenth century, this species was among the most heavily tapped sources of natural rubber across Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, processed into a lower-grade product known as Gutta Rambong; it lost out commercially because Pará rubber could be tapped productively after only about six years of growth, compared with roughly fifteen years needed for Ficus elastica, and by the early twentieth century the Indian rubber tree had essentially been abandoned for industrial latex production. Today it survives commercially only as one of the world's most familiar houseplants and landscape trees, grown in countless variegated and dark-leaved cultivars such as 'Robusta', hardy outdoors only in frost-free zones. Its most striking cultural use is in Meghalaya, in northeastern India, where Khasi and Jaintia communities have for generations guided the tree's living aerial roots across rivers and ravines to grow into functional, weight-bearing living root bridges, some of which have been in continuous use and growth for well over a century.

chunks.source: Singapore Heritage Trees Register (National Parks Board) — Indian Rubber Tree, HT 2010-181
chunks.text: This official heritage-tree citation documents a single, specific Ficus elastica standing in front of the National Museum of Singapore, recorded with a girth of 19.75 metres and a height of 18.6 metres, and traceable in photographs and postcards back to at least 1955, which gives it protected status as a tree of historic and civic significance rather than simply an old specimen. The citation repeats the same historical thread found in broader botanical sources — that the species' latex was once tapped and processed locally into Gutta Rambong, a rubber considered inferior once Pará rubber from Brazil became available and could be tapped in a fraction of the time — but grounds that history in a specific colonial-era landscape, noting that the tree's roots have grown directly over the remnants of the old perimeter fence that once enclosed the Raffles Museum and Library, the institution's predecessor. The entry frames the tree as a literal living link between Singapore's botanical, economic and institutional history: a reminder that ornamental or heritage trees standing today in public squares were very often also, within living or near-living memory, working economic plants grown and tapped for trade before being superseded by better alternatives elsewhere.
